strengths: The paper makes a useful contribution to watermarking discrete-token autoregressive image generators. Grouping nearby codebook entries addresses a concrete failure mechanism: image perturbations change reconstructed token identities, making ordinary red-green watermarking fragile. The training-free method and optional cluster classifier are straightforward and well motivated.

The main experiments demonstrate substantial gains across two generator families and three configurations. In Table 1, clustering raises LlamaGen GPT-B JPEG detection TPR at 1% FPR from 0.680 to 0.959. Adding the classifier raises Gaussian-noise TPR from 0.414 to 0.900 and salt-and-pepper TPR from 0.427 to 0.999. Comparisons include the concurrent IndexMark method on LlamaGen.

The ablations meaningfully investigate cluster count, watermark strength, green fraction, and variability across eight prefixes. Reporting both selected-prefix results and across-prefix statistics helps reveal the robustness–quality tradeoff. Image quality is evaluated with 50,000 generated samples per setting.

Verification is practical: Table 2 reports approximately 10–24 ms per image without generator inference or diffusion inversion. Overall, the demonstrated robustness improvements and simple integration provide a stronger case for acceptance than the remaining limitations provide for rejection.
weaknesses: The statistical detection formulation is not adequately justified. Repeated cluster transitions reuse the same green assignments, and nonuniform cluster frequencies can invalidate the Binomial(T, gamma) null; Section 4.3 explicitly observes deviations. Empirical ROC evaluation still supports discrimination on the tested distribution, but does not validate the advertised binomial p-values. False-positive calibration is evaluated only against 2,000 same-generator negatives, without establishing control on real images, other generators, or perturbed negatives.

Prefix selection lacks a clearly independent final evaluation split. Appendix A.6 selects prefixes using the generated evaluation samples, and Table 7 reports their selected performance. Selecting on perturbation set A and evaluating stronger set B provides some separation, but image-level independence is unspecified and regeneration attacks are shared. Across-prefix statistics mitigate this concern, but selected-prefix deployment performance remains less securely established.

The classifier's specific advantage over perturbation-trained token reconstruction is not isolated. IndexMark is included, but there is no matched token-classifier control trained with the same data and augmentations. Given the acknowledged related work on semantic clustering and robust token reconstruction, this limits attribution of the classifier gains specifically to cluster prediction.

Robustness claims should remain scoped to the tested transformations. Geometric misalignment is acknowledged but not quantified, and averaging two autoencoder reconstructions with a diffusion regeneration attack obscures performance against each distinct attack. The quality cost is also meaningful for RAR-XL: FID rises from 3.13 to 3.96 at the main operating point.

Reproducibility and presentation need refinement. The manuscript omits optimizer and learning-rate details for classifier training. Table 7 sometimes changes the selected prefix between clustering and classifier variants while retaining identical FID values, leaving unclear whether quality was measured for the corresponding prefix. Separately, Section 2.2 reverses the p-value rejection inequality, and Algorithm 1 counts h·w−1 transitions while using h·w binomial trials. These latter errors are readily correctable, but should be distinguished from the substantive calibration concern.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete obstacle to transferring red-green watermarking to image generation: decoding, re-encoding, and perturbations change discrete token identities. Clustering codebook embeddings and predicting clusters directly are coherent solutions that exploit visual-token similarity.

Table 1 demonstrates substantial improvements over direct token watermarking. On LlamaGen GPT-B, clustering raises TPR@1% FPR under JPEG-20 from 0.680 to 0.959 and under regeneration from 0.710 to 0.972. The cluster classifier further raises Gaussian-noise TPR from 0.414 to 0.900 and salt-and-pepper TPR from 0.427 to 0.999. Improvements across two model families support the central contribution.

The evaluation includes extensive sweeps over cluster count, watermark strength, green fraction, and eight prefixes, with mean and standard deviation reported in the supplement. Comparing against IndexMark with its reconstruction encoder enabled is useful. Training on unwatermarked images and testing perturbations stronger than several training settings also strengthen the evidence.

The method has practical appeal: its basic version needs no training, the classifier changes only verification, and measured verification takes approximately 10–24 ms. FID evaluation uses 50,000 generated images. Overall, these supported methodological and empirical contributions favor weak acceptance despite the calibration and evaluation reservations below.
weaknesses: The statistical detection formulation is not adequately justified. Repeated cluster transitions reuse the same deterministic green assignments, so green-token indicators need not be independent Bernoulli trials. Figure 5 explicitly shows prefix-dependent departures from the assumed null mean. Empirical ROC evaluation still supports discrimination on the tested data, but it does not validate Algorithm 1's binomial p-values or deployment false-positive guarantees. Negatives are generated, unwatermarked images; Figure 5 explicitly uses unperturbed negatives. False positives on real images, other generators, and perturbed negatives remain unestablished.

Prefix selection lacks a clearly documented independent validation/test split. Appendix A.6 and Table 7 select the best of eight prefixes using the reported detection evaluations. Selecting on perturbation set A and evaluating stronger set B provides some separation, but independence of the underlying images is unspecified, and regeneration attacks are shared between sets. The across-prefix results mitigate this concern, but selected-prefix performance may be optimistic.

The regeneration column averages SD1.5 and FLUX autoencoder round trips together with an SD2.1 diffusion regeneration attack. These are materially different attacks, and the aggregate conceals performance on each, particularly the diffusion attack. Geometric robustness is explicitly unsupported, and adaptive removal or spoofing is not evaluated; the evidence therefore supports a narrower robustness claim than general resistance to watermark attacks.

Originality is primarily in the particular adaptation and empirical study. Section 5 acknowledges semantic clustering for language watermarking, concurrent clustering for image watermarking, and perturbation-trained token reconstructors. An otherwise matched perturbation-trained full-token classifier would help isolate the benefit of predicting clusters from the benefit of robust encoder training. The current comparisons establish system-level gains more clearly than this component-level distinction.

Quality preservation and reproducibility need more qualification. At the main setting, RAR-XL FID rises from 3.13 to 3.96, a meaningful trade-off despite the strong detection gains. Optimizer, learning rate, and precise classifier-head specifications are not supplied in the manuscript. Separately, correctable presentation errors include rejecting the null when the p-value 'exceeds' the threshold and using h·w binomial trials despite counting only h·w−1 transitions; these errors alone would not determine rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem in autoregressive image watermarking: decoding and re-encoding, especially after perturbations, changes token identities and undermines direct transfer of text watermarking. Assigning visually similar tokens to the same cluster provides a coherent and simple solution.

Table 1 supports substantial gains from clustering and cluster classification across two model families and three configurations. For LlamaGen GPT-L, Gaussian-noise TPR at 1% FPR increases from 0.097 without clustering to 0.460 with clustering and 0.947 with the classifier. The corresponding salt-and-pepper results improve from 0.090 to 0.518 to 1.000.

The experimental study includes meaningful component comparisons, cluster-count and watermark-strength ablations, statistics across eight prefixes, and FID evaluation using 50,000 generated images. Supplementary results across prefixes strengthen the evidence beyond the selected configurations.

The method offers practical advantages: its base variant requires no training, the classifier changes only verification, and reported verification takes approximately 10–24 milliseconds per image. These supported contributions favor acceptance despite the calibration and evaluation limitations.
weaknesses: The statistical detection formulation is not adequately justified. Repeated cluster transitions and nonuniform cluster frequencies need not produce independent Bernoulli trials with probability gamma for a fixed key; Figure 5 itself shows departures from the assumed null mean. Empirical ROC evaluation remains informative, but does not validate Algorithm 1's binomial p-values. Separately, the rejection inequality in Section 2.2 is reversed, and Algorithm 1 counts h*w−1 transitions while using h*w trials.

False-positive validation is restricted to 2,000 unwatermarked images from the corresponding generator, with Figure 5 explicitly using unperturbed negatives. False-positive behavior on real images, other generators, and perturbed negatives is untested. Prefix selection uses measured robustness on perturbation set A, but an independent image split for selection and final evaluation is not documented. Set B's stronger perturbations provide some separation, although the regeneration attacks are shared.

The classifier comparison does not fully isolate the benefit of predicting clusters: there is no matched token-reconstruction classifier trained with the same data and augmentations. The paper acknowledges closely related concurrent clustering and reconstruction approaches, so the originality lies primarily in this particular formulation and its empirical analysis.

Robustness has clear limits. Geometric transformations are acknowledged as unsupported but are not quantified, and evaluation is confined to ImageNet class-conditioned generation. Averaging two autoencoder attacks and diffusion regeneration into one column also obscures performance against each individual attack.

Image-quality preservation is uneven: the main configuration raises RAR-XL FID from 3.13 to 3.96, whereas the LlamaGen increases are smaller. Reproducibility is helped by the supplementary settings, but optimizer and learning-rate details for classifier training are missing, and the promised code release cannot substitute for information in the submitted manuscript.

strengths: The paper addresses a concrete obstacle to watermarking autoregressive image generators: re-encoding and perturbations change visual token identities. Clustering both the conditioning context and green/red assignments is a simple, technically well-motivated solution, with an optional learned reconstruction stage.

Table 1 provides strong evidence that clustering contributes beyond classifier training alone. On LlamaGen GPT-L, adding clustering to the token-classifier variant improves TPR@1%FPR from 0.550 to 0.991 under blur, 0.698 to 0.925 under Gaussian noise, and 0.729 to 0.991 for the reported regeneration average.

The evaluation covers two generator families, three model configurations, relevant concurrent baselines, and substantial ablations of cluster count, watermark strength, green fraction, prefixes, and clustering initialization. Prefix selection uses separate positive images from the main evaluation, and the supplement explicitly investigates geometric failures and synchronization.

The method has practical advantages: the base version requires no training, learned verification leaves the generator decoder unchanged, and verification takes roughly 10–24 milliseconds. These supported robustness and efficiency contributions favor acceptance despite the calibration and deployment limitations.
weaknesses: The binomial significance test is not adequately justified for repeated, dependent cluster transitions. Section 4.3 itself demonstrates heavy-tailed null distributions and prefix-dependent false positives. Empirical ROC results remain useful, but they do not validate the nominal p-values in Algorithm 1. Evaluation uses only 2,000 same-generator negative images, without demonstrating a fixed calibrated threshold on independent real images or other generators; independence of the negative sets used for prefix selection and final evaluation is also unclear.

Standalone robustness to geometric edits is poor: Table 8 shows near-chance detection for several translations, flips, and rotations. SyncSeal substantially mitigates this limitation, but the combined system's image-quality cost and runtime are not reported alongside its detection results. The practical robustness claim therefore depends partly on an additional component.

The quality–robustness trade-off is understated for RAR-XL: the main clustering configuration increases FID from 3.13 to 3.96, and its training-free TPR is only 0.100 under blur and 0.087 under Gaussian noise. Strong performance on this model depends on the trained classifier; claims about uniformly strong training-free robustness and negligible quality effects should be narrower.

The regeneration column averages two autoencoder round trips with a diffusion regeneration attack, obscuring performance against each individually. TrustMark is also evaluated using its built-in detector rather than the common empirical 1%FPR operating point, limiting the comparability of that baseline.

Originality is primarily in the adaptation and empirical demonstration: semantic clustering already exists in LLM watermarking, reconstruction training appears in concurrent AR methods, and Section 5 mentions another clustering-based AR watermark without explaining its algorithmic distinction in sufficient detail. Reproducibility is additionally limited by missing optimizer and learning-rate details and an absent code URL in the provided manuscript.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem in autoregressive image watermarking: image re-encoding and perturbations disrupt token identity. Assigning nearby codebook tokens to the same watermark cluster is a simple, technically motivated solution that modifies neither the generator backbone nor the decoder.

Table 1 provides convincing evidence that clustering contributes beyond trained token recovery. On LlamaGen GPT-L, adding clustering to the token-classifier variant increases TPR@1%FPR from 0.550 to 0.991 under blur, 0.698 to 0.925 under Gaussian noise, and 0.729 to 0.991 under regeneration. Improvements also extend to RAR-XL and comparisons with IndexMark and WMAR.

The experimental analysis is substantial: three model configurations, training-free and trained variants, clustering and watermark-strength ablations, multiple prefixes, cluster-initialization sensitivity, and 50,000-image FID measurements. The supplement explicitly separates positive images used for parameter selection from the main robustness evaluation.

The method has practical efficiency advantages: verification takes approximately 10–24 milliseconds per image, and reported generation overhead is small. The supplement also demonstrates that integration with SyncSeal can recover detection after several geometric transformations.

Overall, the supported empirical contribution favors weak acceptance. Although the conceptual advance is modest and deployment claims need qualification, the consistent improvements and useful analysis outweigh the limitations.
weaknesses: False-positive calibration is the main technical concern. Repeated cluster transitions under a fixed key invalidate the independent-binomial interpretation of green counts; Section 4.3 explicitly demonstrates heavy-tailed negative distributions. Empirical ROC evaluation still supports discrimination on the tested data, but prefix selection does not establish calibrated p-values or a reliable deployment threshold. Evaluation uses only 2,000 same-generator negative images, without demonstrating false-positive control on real images or other generators.

Native geometric robustness is poor. Table 8 reports near-chance detection for several flips, rotations, and translations. SyncSeal substantially mitigates this limitation, but introduces an additional component whose combined image-quality and runtime costs are not reported. The standalone robustness claims should be distinguished from those of the combined system.

Novelty is primarily an effective adaptation and integration of existing ideas. Semantic clustering for LLM watermarking and trained token recovery are established, and Section 5 acknowledges concurrent clustering-based image watermarking by Wu et al. The manuscript gives little technical explanation of how its clustering formulation differs from that closest approach, weakening the originality argument.

Quality preservation and robustness are not uniform across settings. At the main operating point, RAR-XL FID increases from 3.13 to 3.96, while training-free clustering achieves only 0.100 TPR under blur and 0.087 under Gaussian noise. The strongest robustness therefore depends on additional classifier training, and the quality cost is appreciable for this model.

Some evaluation choices limit interpretation: regeneration averages two autoencoder round trips and a diffusion attack, obscuring their individual difficulty; TrustMark uses its built-in decision rule rather than a matched empirical 1% FPR threshold. All tested generators are ImageNet class-conditioned, so broader text-to-image applicability remains unverified.

Reproducibility is only partial in the supplied manuscript. It provides architectures, sample counts, augmentation settings, batch size, and training duration, but omits optimizer and learning-rate details and leaves the source-code link blank. These are correctable reporting gaps rather than grounds for rejection by themselves.

strengths: The paper makes a useful, well-motivated contribution to watermarking autoregressive image generators. Clustering similar codebook tokens and using cluster identities for both hashing and green-set assignment directly addresses token reconstruction errors introduced by image encoding and perturbations. The training-free variant is simple, and the optional reconstruction classifiers require no changes to the generator or decoder.

Table 1 provides convincing evidence that clustering improves robustness beyond directly transferring KGW. On LlamaGen GPT-L, training-free clustering increases TPR@1% FPR from 0.193 to 0.905 under blur and from 0.812 to 0.997 under regeneration. With a token classifier, RAR-XL achieves 0.885 under Gaussian noise and 0.945 under regeneration, compared with WMAR's 0.476 and 0.758.

The evaluation is substantial: three model configurations across two generator families, relevant concurrent and post-hoc baselines, 50,000-image FID measurements, and ablations over cluster count, watermark strength, green fraction, and hash prefix. The supplement explicitly separates watermarked images used for prefix selection from those used for the main robustness evaluation and examines cluster initialization sensitivity.

The method has practical efficiency advantages: reported verification takes approximately 10–24 ms per image, with small generation overhead. The paper also acknowledges geometric vulnerabilities and supplies meaningful SyncSeal experiments rather than merely suggesting synchronization as future work. Overall, the supported empirical contribution favors acceptance despite the limitations below.
weaknesses: False-positive calibration is the main technical reservation. The binomial null in Section 2.2 and Algorithm 1 assumes behavior that repeated cluster transitions need not satisfy; Sections 3.4 and 4.3 explicitly demonstrate prefix-dependent heavy tails on unwatermarked images. Empirical ROC results remain useful, but selecting a favorable prefix does not establish calibrated p-values. Evaluation uses only 2,000 same-generator negative images, with no demonstrated fixed-threshold false-positive control on real images or other generators. Independence of negative samples used for prefix tuning and final evaluation is also unclear.

The quality–robustness trade-off is meaningful and somewhat understated. At the main operating point, RAR-XL FID increases from 3.13 to 3.96, and GPT-L from 4.50 to 4.85. On RAR-XL, training-free clustering still gives only 0.100 TPR under blur and 0.087 under Gaussian noise; the strong results depend on training a predictor using 100,000 generated images. The paper establishes a useful trade-off, but not uniformly negligible quality loss or strong training-free robustness.

Robustness claims need a bounded interpretation. Unassisted geometric transformations can reduce detection below 10% TPR. SyncSeal substantially mitigates this, but the combined system's image-quality and runtime costs are not quantified. Averaging two autoencoder reconstruction attacks and one diffusion regeneration attack into a single column also obscures attack-specific performance. Adaptive removal and forgery are not evaluated, while Appendix D assumes that the backbone, tokenizer, and predictor remain private.

The originality is primarily the adaptation and empirical validation of a clustering-based watermark in visual token space. Related work already includes semantic clustering for language watermarks and a concurrent clustering-based AR image watermark [39]. The discussion distinguishes the latter mainly through its model and evaluation coverage, leaving the precise algorithmic distinction insufficiently established.

Reproducibility is partially supported by pseudocode and extensive experimental settings, but the supplied manuscript's source-code statement has no link, and classifier training omits optimizer and learning-rate details. Comparison claims also require qualification: TrustMark uses its built-in detection threshold rather than the common empirical 1% FPR operating point. These are correctable reporting limitations, distinct from the substantive calibration concern.
